evidence.fact: Research on deep learning for tree segmentation and species classification from LiDAR is well developed (e.g. transformer classifiers, interactive segmentation pipelines). An agent can write code, run analyses and draft protocols for these methods. The main limit is that individual trees in point clouds must still be labelled to provide ground-truth data, which slows this work down.

Licensing applies to professional forestry practice and recommendations in some states, such as California's RPF signature and stamp rules. These rules do not cover developing measurement or identification methods, so a human signature is not legally required for this task.
Many states do not regulate foresters at all, so licensing barriers vary by state and are limited.

Remote refraction apps such as Opternative, myRx and Warby Parker's Virtual Vision Test can support prescription renewals. A licensed physician still issues or approves each prescription, and the tests only cover narrow patient groups. They are not comprehensive exams.

Under the FTC Contact Lens Rule, a prescriber fits the lenses, releases the prescription at the end of the fitting and keeps signed confirmations. Under the FTC Eyeglass Rule, the prescriber hands over the prescription after an eye exam that includes a refraction. This makes a licensed prescriber accountable for the work.

Online refraction can renew prescriptions with physician approval, but fitting, supplying and adjusting eyeglasses and contact lenses means handling the patient and the device in person. An agent can only help with digital sub-steps such as drafting the prescription, choosing lenses and placing orders.

Consumer AI apps and research prototypes, such as an avatar breathing coach and an SMS or web yoga e-coach, can guide relaxation and breathing exercises. None of them covers recreational therapy practice or clinician-supervised instruction in sports, dance or art.

In Utah, a TRS licence requires a current NCTRC CTRS certification plus a documented practicum. Some states, including New Hampshire, also license recreational therapists, so a human professional is accountable for treatment delivery.

New Hampshire requires a degree, fieldwork supervised by a CTRS and the NCTRC exam to practise. This in-person clinical role involves demonstrating activities and adapting them to the patient as they go.

AI agents settle many routine retail and e-commerce inquiries on digital channels with no human involved. Vendors claim 76–92%, but independent benchmarks put it nearer 14–50%. About 22% of AI-handled tickets are passed to a human, and 58% of consumers are not fully comfortable with AI support.

In-store AI kiosks such as CJ Olive Young's 2026 rollout can answer product, stock and navigation questions in several languages. They are fixed kiosks, though. Greeting shoppers on the floor and handling complaints face to face are still done by staff and supervisors.

Other in-store AI tools, like Skechers' Luna kiosk, mostly support shoppers and store associates with information and suggestions. They do not stand in for the supervisor who handles customers in person on the floor.
Gecko says its AI voice agents for equipment rental answer calls 24/7, collect rental details, quote from live inventory, take bookings and take payment during the call. This is a vendor claim.

OneAI says its car-rental agent checks live availability, quotes total prices including taxes and fees, and books reservations during the call. The vendor's own case figures show bookings from about 38% of contacts.
SendSquared says its AI voice agent checks live availability in the property system, quotes prices and writes confirmed reservations back. It markets this for its Guesty integration.

Endless-aisle and POS software (Shopify POS, Aptos, NewStore, Salesforce Retail Cloud, Retail Express) gives sales associates a view of stock across the whole chain. The associate can place a special order or send the order to the location that holds the item. This is digital work an agent can do through computer use.

Google's agentic 'Let Google Call' feature, built on Duplex, phones nearby stores on its own to check stock, price and promotions, then texts or emails a summary. So the 'call other stores' sub-step is already automated.
Vendors say retail voice agents connect to inventory and CRM systems to handle questions about product availability and order status. Most of the performance claims come from the vendors themselves.

Intuit's 2026 QuickBooks agents read time data, draft pay runs and draft journal entries for wages, taxes and benefits. They are human-in-the-loop by design and need owner approval before anything posts, so the setup sub-steps can be automated but still need human review.

AI agents can pull employee compensation data from payroll records, quarterly reports and tax filings to calculate exposure bases for insurance policies. This shows that mapping insurance data to bookkeeping records is technically within an agent's reach.

The NAIC Producer Licensing Model Act requires a licence only to sell, solicit or negotiate insurance. Administrative work only indirectly tied to sales is exempt, so integrating a policy into bookkeeping is not a licensed act.

AI receptionist products for law firms answer inbound calls, run intake and conflict checks against the case-management system, and book consultations. They send urgent matters to an on-call attorney and do not give legal advice, so a human still takes the sensitive or judgment-heavy calls.
In 2026 there are many AI voice agents built for law firms that work as 24/7 virtual receptionists. Examples include Smith.ai, Lindy and Voiceflow, and some combine AI with human staff.

The FCC's February 2024 ruling places AI-generated voices under the TCPA's rules for an 'artificial or prerecorded voice'. Some outbound calls therefore need consent and must identify the caller. This is a rule on how calls are made, not a ban, and it does not require a human to make the calls.

SAP released a rebuilt Ariba with built-in agent features in March 2026 and plans to add 11 Joule agents across Ariba and Fieldglass during 2026. Coupa has more than 20 role-based agents and launched Coupa Compose to build and run agents, and its September 2026 release lets agents run sourcing and payment workflows on their own.

Analysts say the 'autonomous' label is overstated. Cross-module agent workflows still need testing, and approval limits remain a barrier, so a human still sets the rules and approves configuration changes.

Governance guidance tells firms to set spending thresholds, list the decisions that need human review and keep explainable audit trails. These come from internal delegation-of-authority rules and the EU AI Act's high-risk rules, not from any licence that requires a human signature.
O*NET lists this as a Food Service Manager task: cooking, clearing tables and serving food and drinks when needed. All of it is hands-on physical work in the kitchen and dining room.
Restaurants that automate serving or bussing use dedicated robots such as Bear Robotics' Servi. That is physical hardware, outside the reference technology of software-only AI agents with no body.
Restaurant automation trends for 2026 point to robots, not software agents, as the answer to labor shortages in cooking and service.

Vendors sell AI agents for aerospace task management and team collaboration. Their own pitch says the agents handle repetitive tasks while humans review and approve the output. That means the agents help with scheduling, tracking and status reporting, but they do not direct engineering staff.

In 2026, NASA and Airbus are using agentic AI to automate design-variant generation and design-to-cost workflows. This automates the technical work being supervised, not the coordination of the people doing it.

The FAA appoints qualified individuals (Designated Engineering Representatives, who must hold an engineering degree under 14 CFR 183.29) to find that engineering data meets airworthiness standards. This puts accountability for design and test outcomes on humans.

Celanese's JO.AI agents are used across about 50 plants. They handle shift checklists, flag anomalies and draft work orders. Operators and managers still direct the work, so the agents help supervision rather than replace it.
ControlRooms released a multi-agent system in September 2026 that handles detection, advice, logging and shift handover summaries. The vendor stresses that humans stay in the loop to oversee safety.

OSHA's process safety rule (PSM, 29 CFR 1910.119) requires trained operators and an employee participation plan. Directing production in hazardous chemical processes happens on the plant floor and relies on people supervising people in person.

Epic's Chart with Art: Nursing, live at Mount Sinai and other systems in 2026, drafts the end-of-shift care plan notes from chart data (vitals, flowsheets, medications) and from ambient capture at the bedside. Drafts go into the chart only after the clinician reviews them. Mercy reported note time falling from 3.5 minutes to about 32 seconds (a vendor-reported figure).

Under the College of Nurses of Ontario documentation standard, effective February 2026, nurses may use AI for documentation. They remain accountable for everything entered into the record and must review and verify all AI-generated content.
BCCNM standards require nurses to sign each entry in the client record to show accountability, whether the entry was written by hand or generated electronically.

Under 42 CFR 482.13(e)-(f), only trained, authorized staff may restrain a patient, and only when the patient's immediate physical safety is at risk. That staff must be trained to apply restraints safely, watch for distress such as positional asphyxia, and de-escalate. In practice this means trained people physically handle and watch the patient.

AI video and wearable systems that predict aggression or agitation on psychiatric wards are still small pilots or proofs of concept. At most they send alerts. None of them can physically restrain or help a patient.
Legal and ethical reviews urge caution before using AI-CCTV monitoring on mental health wards, citing privacy and consent. This limits AI to a narrow advisory role.

Commercial visitor-management and access-control systems already handle pre-registration, face-matched check-in with liveness detection, badge issuing and entry/exit audit trails, in some cases without reception staff. The remaining work is mostly physical: intercepting tailgaters, inspecting bags or vehicles and confronting people.
Face-recognition visitor modules let administrators set when and where each visitor may enter and can enroll unexpected visitors on-site, which automates the authorization step.

US states license security guards individually (for example California's Guard Card, Texas Level II and Tennessee). In many states a person cannot work as a contract security officer without a state license.
Line cook work during service means grilling, sautéing, prepping mise en place and plating by hand. Cooking robots are limited to narrow fast-food uses and cannot yet adapt to unexpected variables.
As of October 2026, cooking robots still cannot handle unexpected variables on the fly, and some deployments have failed. In any case, the reference agents have no robotic body.
Several states, including Illinois, require anyone handling food in a restaurant to hold an accredited food handler certificate. This is a credential tied to a person.

AI voice and kiosk ordering (Square's AI kiosk launched in October 2026; Taco Bell drive-thru voice AI is in more than 100 locations) handles order taking and payment. It does not do the physical packaging or hand food to customers.
Taco Bell says more than 100 locations in 13 states use voice AI at the drive-thru. This software takes the order, but the food is still assembled and handed over by people.
Food Code rules require hands-on handling of ready-to-eat food with utensils or gloves. Packaging and serving are physical tasks, though the code does not require a human to sign anything.

Self-pour beer walls and robotic dispensers (iPourIt, Pubinno, PourMyBeer) handle draft dispensing with hardware, RFID cards and POS links, not software-only AI agents. Guests still pour, or a staff member checks ID in person, so the physical serving stays with people or machines.
Pubinno sells AI-powered devices and robotics that automate draft beer dispensing. That shows the automation that exists needs a physical body, which the reference agents do not have.

California requires bartenders and other alcohol servers to hold Responsible Beverage Service certification, which includes training on checking IDs. Other states have similar rules, so a human must be accountable for serving alcohol.

Several vendors (Spatula, Perklist, Nora Neo, Mimiway, QRSur) offer AI menu assistants that diners open from a table QR code. They say these answer menu, ingredient and allergen questions and recommend dishes, wine pairings and add-ons in many languages. These are vendors' own descriptions and have not been independently checked. Some say the assistant only uses allergen data the restaurant has confirmed, so a human still has to maintain and confirm that data.
Vendors present AI menu assistants as taking over routine questions so staff can focus on in-person hospitality. Handing over menus at the table and reading guests in person still need a human there.

The 2022 FDA Food Code (§3-602.12(C)) requires written notice of major allergens for unpackaged food, and the notice can be electronic. These searches found no rule requiring a licensed human to answer menu questions. One Illinois bill would require menus to tell allergic guests to notify a waiter, but the results don't confirm it was enacted.

Childcare platforms such as Brightwheel already have digital daily reports where staff log naps, meals, bathroom use and activities, and the app compiles them into summaries for families. They also include tools for observations and assessments against state standards.

Childcare software vendors now offer AI that turns teachers' brief observations into narrative updates and translations, but a teacher must approve each post before it is published. Practitioner guidance says AI should only tidy what a person observed, and that medication, accident and safeguarding records should never be written by AI.

Licensing rules require each dose of medication to be logged with the child's name, the dose, the date and time, and the staff member who gave it. California's medication chart has a staff signature line for each entry, so a human must perform and attest to it.

AI companions such as ElliQ can provide conversation and reminders to older adults. New York's state pilot with the maker reached more than 800 people, and 95% of users said it reduced their loneliness. That figure is self-reported, not from a controlled study. This covers only the companionship part of the task, which a device can supplement, not replace.

State rules define personal care as hands-on work: bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, transfers, positioning in bed, feeding and help with walking. All of it requires a person to be physically there.

States such as New York require at least 40 hours of training plus demonstrated skills, which shows the role depends on a trained human being present in person. These rules set competency standards; they do not require anyone to sign off on the care.

Librarians already use AI chatbots and design tools for the digital parts of display work: picking themes, building themed booklists and read-alikes, finding quotes and making signage. These tools help with the work but do not set up the display.

State library guidance treats AI as an optional tool that sparks ideas and speeds up tasks, not a replacement for staff. Editable bookmark reading lists and poster templates in Canva support display signage.

Library assistant job descriptions combine arranging and maintaining displays with physical work: pulling books from shelves, lifting and carrying materials, pushing trolleys and reaching above shoulder height. This part is physical and needs a person on site.

Motorola Solutions' Dispatcher Assist Suite produces real-time transcripts of radio traffic. Its Assist product prepares incidents from transcribed radio traffic, but a dispatcher must confirm them before they count.

Hobbyist tools such as Scanner Command transcribe live scanner audio with Whisper, use AI to pull out what happened and where, and map incidents automatically. The core monitoring sub-steps can be automated.

AI transcription of radio feeds makes mistakes that matter. In Bend, Oregon, 'Shop with a Cop' was transcribed as 'shot with a cop' and set off false alerts. A human still needs to review the output before acting on it.

The Weather Company's Operations Dashboard for Ground Transportation (2017 coverage) combines weather, road conditions and live traffic and incident data. It sends drivers real-time hazard alerts for their current and upcoming locations, and dispatchers can push custom alerts to drivers through an API.

WeatherOptics, sold through the Motive and Samsara marketplaces, can automatically alert drivers in real time to weather hazards and suggest actions such as slowing down, pulling over or taking another route.
Lytx Weather Hazard Alerts uses AI-powered geospatial technology and NOAA data, and fleet managers can set alerts by place, time window and weather type. It covers weather, not traffic.

OpenAI's Deep Research agent plans and carries out multi-step web research by itself. It backtracks when needed and returns a report with citations in 5 to 30 minutes. This is the core of the task. The coverage found dates from the 2025 launch, so current limits may differ.
ChatGPT agent combines Deep Research with Operator. It can navigate websites, filter results, ask the user to log in when needed, run code, and produce editable documents or spreadsheets.

Agents that search and synthesize hundreds of online sources into research-level reports were commercially available well before October 2026. The task needs no physical presence and no licence or signature. These two points are a judgement from the task's nature; I did not search them separately.

Adobe's InDesign AI Assistant takes plain-language requests and carries out multi-step layout changes. It is still in beta, so it can make modifications from instructions, but the documentation does not show it judging rendered pages visually.

Computer-use agents work in a loop: take a screenshot, decide what to do, act, then check the result and correct it. This matches viewing the work in progress on screen and fixing it. The source describes the general pattern and does not mention InDesign.

Design agents in Figma and Framer build layouts from components and accept screenshots as references. The work is done entirely in software, so no physical presence is needed. Final aesthetic judgment and acting on client feedback usually still go through a human.

In InDesign, the Separations Preview panel and Ink Manager let a user turn spot colors into CMYK, decide which inks get their own plate, and check ink-coverage limits, all in software. An agent that can operate a desktop could run these steps. Adobe still advises checking with the printer before converting brand inks.

Esko Equinox, a prepress tool, converts spot colors into a fixed process ink set (CMYK plus up to three extra inks). The vendor says this makes the choice of ink count and separations predictable. These claims come from Esko, not independent tests.

Choosing how many colors to use is a trade-off between budget, brand accuracy and the press. Results depend on the printer's own press setup and need proofing. In practice a human usually confirms the choice with the client or printer, but no licence or legal sign-off is required.

Repair-shop estimating software already automates labor and parts calculations using labor guides and pricing matrices, and vendors claim AI can generate estimates from historical repair orders. These are vendor claims, not independent results.
Estimating tools pull parts availability and supplier pricing straight into estimates, work orders and invoices, so collecting cost data is a software job.

CMMS tools record planned against actual labor hours and material costs and produce variance reports, but they depend on technicians entering accurate time and materials, which is often guessed after the job. A human still has to judge the scope of the job and verify contractor invoices.

O*NET (49-9044.00) lists this as a core millwright task, rated 73/100 in importance. Millwrights install, take apart and move heavy machinery, which involves hands-on rigging, alignment, shimming and shrink-fitting.

Employer job postings describe the duty as taking equipment apart for transport and sharing installation and upkeep with a crew. The work uses hoists, lift trucks, rigging, leveling and foundation building, so it needs physical presence.

The available digital tools give AR step-by-step instructions to guide human technicians through disassembly and reassembly. A software agent can help with documentation and sequence planning, but it cannot do the physical work.

O*NET says helpers work hands-on, assisting with maintenance, parts replacement and repair of vehicles, industrial machinery and electrical equipment, and lists examining and testing machinery and parts for defects among their tasks.
AI vibration-analysis tools flag obvious defects from collected sensor data so analysts can focus on harder cases. The vendor presents the tool as helping analysts rather than replacing them.
Cloud ML platforms find anomalies in sensor data, but experienced analysts review the results. The sensors have to be physically installed on the machines first.

Parking guidance systems already direct drivers to free spaces without an attendant. Sensors in each space detect occupancy and feed LED indicators and directional signs. These are fixed sensor and signage systems, not AI agents, and they only work in garages that have them installed.

Guidance signage at major intersections inside a garage sends drivers only down rows with free spaces. This does the wayfinding part of the job through installed infrastructure rather than a software agent.

The task as described means a person standing in the lot and directing cars with hand signals or a flashlight. An agent with no body cannot do that. Searches found no licence requirement for this work, though I did not run a search aimed specifically at licensing law.

Instantly says its AI SDR agent finds leads, writes and sends personalized outreach emails, follows up and books meetings to a rep's calendar without a person. This is the vendor's own marketing claim.
Relevance AI's marketplace lists AI agents for outbound email and meeting booking. They contact organizations, explain what is offered and book qualified meetings directly. The page is promotional.

Independent reviews of AI SDR tools say autonomy varies. Some tools only run sequences that humans design, and the reviewers point to a big gap between sending emails in bulk and getting qualified meetings. That supports keeping a human to review the messaging and to build the relationship.

AI benefits decision-support products are on the market in 2026. HealthJoy's tool estimates each plan's annual cost and recommends one. Alight's generative AI assistant helps employees compare plans and set HSA/FSA contributions. A published 2026 blueprint for an AI enrollment agent still keeps confirmation steps and hands judgment calls to HR, so humans stay in the loop.

Pave, Decusoft, MangoApps and Salary.com sell AI compensation tools. They generate merit recommendations within budget, flag pay-equity risks and explain their reasoning to managers. Pave's agent is described as an AI compensation analyst. This means an agent could prototype and configure guidance tools. Managing the design work still involves human steps: getting stakeholders and the pay philosophy aligned, choosing a vendor, and approving the result.

The research found that employers are expected to provide an easy path to a human counselor and to review AI recommendations before use. No licence or signature requirement applies to the work of designing these tools, and none of it needs physical presence.

Automated decline-curve analysis already exists. It combines Arps empirical models with AI models such as gradient boosting and LSTM, then extends production to an economic limit. That covers the main sub-steps of forecasting production and value.

An SPE session in 2026 says engineers use generative AI such as Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT for decline-curve, type-curve and economic modeling. It warns that a working prototype is not a production-ready analysis, so a human still has to review the result.

Manual decline-curve analysis depends on the engineer's judgement and is subjective. This supports partial delegation: an agent can do much of the work, but an expert still needs to validate the forecasts. A formal sign-off by a qualified reserves estimator mainly applies to booked reserves, not to internal screening of drilling sites.

Nava's open-source form-filling assistant is being piloted with caseworkers in Riverside County, California. It moves through benefit portals and databases and fills in application forms on its own. Caseworkers still review the forms, add missing information and submit them.

In a March 2026 report on the California pilot, frontline staff said they spend about half their time getting through benefit applications. The AI fills in the forms, but a human checks them before submission.

Agents that guide clients through assistance applications in plain language, including in Spanish and other languages, already exist, such as Link Health. Coverage of AI tax filing says most current work automates only part of tax preparation rather than handling the whole job.

Vendor and FDA-cleared software already automates much of the image processing and quantification. Examples are Cedars-Sinai Cardiac Suite (QPS/QGS with motion correction), AutoQUANT, Siemens xSPECT Quant and GE's MIM portfolio. The technologist still checks and corrects the output, for example ROI and contour placement and motion artifacts.
GE HealthCare showed AI-driven nuclear medicine imaging and quantification software at SNMMI 2026, so these tools are current and on the market.

The SNMMI scope of practice includes operating imaging and computer instrumentation and documenting procedures. Technologists must follow federal, state and institutional rules, and state licensure governs who may perform these duties. The interpretation is signed by the physician, not the technologist.
A pallbearer is one of several people who physically carry the casket at a funeral, usually in a team of four to six, depending on how heavy the coffin is.
Pallbearers move the casket from the hearse into the service and back, then from the hearse to the grave, following the funeral director's instructions in person.
The role is a solemn, ceremonial one: bearers hold the casket at their sides and arrive early to coordinate with the funeral director. This needs a physical body and a human presence before mourners.

Vendor AI BDR and cold-call script tools pull CRM data, buying signals and web research to write a tailored opener, talking points and objection prep for each prospect before the call. These capabilities are vendor-claimed, not independently verified.
Several products say they follow the conversation and suggest talking points live, or adjust scripts based on how the prospect reacts. There is little independent evidence on how reliable this is.

Off-the-shelf tools such as EasyCallScript are sold as giving live call scripts tailored to each lead. I found no licensing or sign-off rule requiring a human to write or adjust sales scripts (not separately searched). Rules such as the TCPA govern consent and disclosures on the call, not who writes the script.

State internal control standards require physical cage protections that people carry out and answer for: restricted keys kept in locked boxes with access logs reviewed before each shift ends, cage doors and windows secured against unauthorized access, and surveillance verification of each cashier's transactions.

Indiana regulators disciplined a casino after cashiers made even exchanges without notifying surveillance and a cage supervisor moved $10,000 without requesting surveillance coverage. The required procedure is that the cage requests a security escort and security requests surveillance coverage, so these steps are in-person and coordinated by staff.

AI in casinos is mostly used for transaction and video anomaly detection that sends alerts to security staff. This helps with monitoring but does not physically secure the cage or replace cashier control of cash and keys.

Under Maine law, a licensed helper electrician may do electrical installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician, and the master electrician is responsible for the work of the people they supervise.
A city job description for an electrician helper lists hands-on maintenance and repair work that a journey-level electrician inspects. The work happens on site.

The search found no software or AI agent that inspects or tightens connections. The task means seeing, touching and turning screws on the equipment itself, which a software-only agent with no body cannot do. This point is a judgment, not a cited finding.
Beach equipment rental software such as Booqable already runs online booking, live availability, deposits and e-signed waivers, so the transaction side of renting can be done without a person.
Bookyt treats each numbered beach chair as its own rental item, so the system can allocate and track chairs automatically. A person still has to set up and hand over the chair.

Self-service kiosks linked to the Lightspeed point-of-sale system handle scheduling and rentals in store, but handing over the physical items (shoes, balls, chairs, suits) still needs someone on site.

AI tools such as Beam AI and Civils.ai already read HVAC blueprints and schedules to pull out duct sizes, lengths and fittings. Vendors say a human still has to check the results, and the tools do not do 3D coordination or clash detection. No 2026 tool was found that turns blueprints into finished shop drawings without a human checking them.
CAD add-ins such as Design Master HVAC already lay out ductwork automatically and size ducts inside AutoCAD or BricsCAD. An agent with computer use could run these tools to draft much of the work.

Standard HVAC duct specifications require scaled fabrication drawings showing fittings, reinforcement, seams and hangers. They are submitted to the engineer of record for review, and no PE seal by the drafter is generally required.

Students in qualitative methods courses used custom GPTs, including an interview simulator, to get quick feedback on interview questions and field notes. This counts as assisting supervision, not replacing the supervisor.
Cogniti lets educators set up AI agents that act as a qualitative methods mentor and give students feedback on how they code their data. The educator still controls the agent and stays in the loop.
University IRB rules make the faculty advisor responsible for how student human-subjects research is carried out, and require the advisor to sign protocols. A human must keep oversight.

Vendor AI tools for medical education say they draft syllabi, learning objectives, curriculum maps, modular course content, review questions and accreditation paperwork from goal specifications. These claims are the vendors' own and have not been checked independently.

Lecturio says its AI syllabus and lesson plan generator drafts competency-aligned syllabi and session plans for health sciences faculty. Its workload-reduction figures are self-reported. AAMC warns against relying too much on AI without enough human oversight.

Accreditation criteria require faculty to take part. In this AACN crosswalk of CCNE standards and NTF criteria, faculty must take part in program governance and quality improvement, and NP faculty must give input into developing, evaluating and revising the curriculum. That means human faculty judgment and sign-off stay essential.

Echometer's wireless Base Station records liquid level, dynamometer and pressure data. A user runs it through TAM software on a laptop or at the sensor, and the software can analyze the acoustic liquid-level data automatically. An agent could do the interpretation if it can reach the digital traces.

Echometer's 2024 equipment comparison says a laptop running TAM software must be present for data acquisition. This means the gun still has to be attached to the wellhead and the shot run on site, so the task is not fully remote.

Automatic echometers such as the SUDOS-automat 2 measure liquid level without an operator and send the data by GSM to a remote database. This shows that monitoring can be digitized and done remotely where such equipment is installed.

Agency staff justify proposed regulation changes with harvest data and population models. In Alaska, a moose model projected harvest by age class to test proposed hunting rules. This kind of data analysis and model-based drafting is work an AI agent can do.

Biologists and field staff submit regulation proposals, a board or commission votes on them after public comment, and the final decision belongs to the commission. Field staff recommend, so their recommendations need no licensed human signature, but they draw on firsthand field observation.
Agencies already use AI tools to summarize public comments that feed into staff regulation recommendations.

Local codes (e.g., Dayton and Fort Mitchell, KY) let a hearing board consider a written report made under oath by the issuing officer in place of personal testimony. The sworn witness must still be the human officer, though an AI could draft or assemble the report.
In Fort Worth the issuing officer is not required to attend the hearing. When the officer does appear, they testify as a fact witness about what they personally saw, which an AI agent cannot do.
A contestant can require the officer who wrote the ticket to attend the hearing. Live witness testimony in court needs a human to be present and under oath.

AI treat dispensers like CompanionPro and a Jetson Nano prototype can recognize and reward simple behaviors. Their makers describe them as aids to a trainer, not stand-alone trainers. They cannot teach assistance or protection tasks, which need hands-on handling, so the agent's role is limited to planning, logging and analyzing video.
Service dog training is typically at least 120 hours of hands-on schooling over six months or more, including 30 hours in public places. This requires a person to be physically present with the dog.
The ADA does not require service dogs to be certified or professionally trained. No law requires a licensed human to perform or sign off on the training.

Virginia's rules say multiuse tools such as clippers, scissors and combs must be washed with hot soapy water, rinsed and fully immersed in disinfectant for at least 10 minutes before use on a client. This is hands-on physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.

California requires removing visible debris from clippers and other electrical tools and then disinfecting them before each use with an EPA-registered spray or wipe. Every step involves handling the tools by hand.

Arkansas requires cleaning by physically removing debris, then disinfecting with an EPA-registered product that kills bacteria, viruses and fungi, before any tool touches a client. The board's sanitation rules hold the licensee responsible but do not require a human signature. The real barrier is physical.

STgenetics' web-based Chromosomal Mating program uses linear programming to assign sires to females. It controls inbreeding and lethal haplotypes while maximizing the predicted producing value of offspring, so the semen-selection sub-step is already done by software.
Viking Genetics' VikMate mating plan tracks inbreeding back six generations and builds a sire list from the semen doses held in storage. It covers the pedigree and trait-matching work in this task.

In BoviSync, mating recommendations are produced by genetic advisors using mating software and then imported into herd-management systems. A human advisor or breeder still sets the breeding goals and accepts the plan, and choosing which animals to breed still relies on on-farm observation of the animals.

Fully automated wool harvesting is still at the proof-of-concept stage. AWI funded Ranken Research and Robo Shear to build a prototype machine, which would be dedicated robotic hardware, not a software agent.

Research on semi-autonomous shearing treats it as a physical job: restraining the animal and guiding the cutter over it. Even the most advanced robot work still needs hand clipping for the head and tail areas.
Later automation work moved to handling wool after shearing, such as trimming dirty wool, classing and baling, using physical robots. None of it can be done through software alone.

Loading an insemination gun is hands-on lab work. The worker takes the straw out of liquid nitrogen with forceps, thaws it in a 35°C water bath, wipes it dry, puts it into the gun, cuts it about 7 mm below the crimp, and then warms or protects the loaded gun. A software-only agent can't do any of these steps.

The setup also needs physical adjustment. The plunger is pushed until it touches the cotton plug, a protective sheath is fitted over the gun, and semen is pushed forward until it just shows at the tip. Automated straw-filling machines exist, but they are mechanical equipment and not AI agents.

The steps differ by species. One source says to cut the straw at the sealed end and not the cotton end. An AI could only help by looking up the right protocol, which is a very small share of the work.

O*NET lists this task for Helpers--Carpenters as cleaning work areas, machines or equipment by hand on the job site. It is manual work. An agent can only add minor digital help, such as checklists or scheduling dumpster pickups.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.25 requires that scrap lumber with protruding nails and other debris be physically cleared from work areas, passageways and stairs, and that waste be put in containers and removed at regular intervals. This needs someone on site. The rule is a duty on the employer and does not require a licensed person to do or sign the cleanup.
Cleaning whitewalls is hands-on work: put a whitewall-safe cleaner on the tire, scrub the sidewall with a brush or pad, then rinse. A software agent with no body can't do any of these steps.
For stubborn yellowing, sources suggest scrubbing with a Scotch-Brite pad or sanding with fine-grit paper. Both need a person (or robot) handling the tire.
The guidance is about picking a safe product, such as avoiding bleach and ammonia. An AI could only help a little by looking up which product to use, which isn't a substantial part of the task.

Job postings for underground linemen describe the work as physical field labor. Crews dig trenches, pull cable by hand from truck-mounted reels or with winches, rod and rope through conduit, and run trenchers, backhoes and bucket trucks. A software-only AI agent can't do any of this.

Underground lineman roles require splicing and terminating URD cable, setting up work zones, wearing PPE and lifting about 50 lb. These steps happen on site, and the paperwork or mapping reports that an agent could help with are a small part of the job.
Utility contractor postings list laying cable in trenches or pulling it through conduit, then backfilling and restoring the site, as core field duties for the line crew.

Under 10 CFR 50.54(k), an operator licensed under Part 55 must be present at the controls at all times while the facility operates. Under 50.54(i), only licensed operators may manipulate controls that affect reactivity or power.

Current AI tools for nuclear plants are decision-support and document assistants that inform plant staff, not systems with control authority. Examples are Argonne's PRO-AID for monitoring and diagnostics and Atomic Canyon's NIVA.

AI agents that suggest control-rod adjustments exist only as research prototypes (Texas A&M). Developers still have to solve sensor and controller latency, and the agents are not deployed in plant control loops.

As of September 2026, SmartBOL's inbound module uses AI to classify and extract data from shipping documents and check each line against the purchase order. This covers the document side of checking loads against work orders.

Camera systems at dock doors count cases, read labels and compare them with expected order data. They need cameras installed on site, and staff still handle the flagged exceptions, so a software-only agent depends on that hardware or on a person doing the physical inspection.

PackageX says it matches 95% of blind receipts and sends low-confidence items to a person for review. These figures come from the vendor, which supports rating this as partial rather than full delegation.

Project44's AI Freight Procurement Agent, part of its Intelligent TMS, compares carriers on cost, transit time and reliability. Depending on configurable rules, it either recommends an award or makes it, and customers can start in recommendation-only mode.
Agentic TMS platforms re-plan continuously and handle routine dispatch and allocation decisions automatically, but material decisions still go to a human for approval.

In 2026, most freight workflows run in copilot mode, where a human approves quotes above a threshold. AI is used for mode selection and load consolidation, but there is little sign of fully autonomous mode selection in production.

AutoScheduler.AI says its decision agents automate warehouse task sequencing, labor scheduling and dock management, and reorder tasks when trucks are late. It adds these agents to an existing WMS rather than replacing it. These are vendor claims.

A trade article says agents need WMS, TMS and ERP data to be connected to see the full picture. The supervisor normally works in these systems, so an agent can reach the same orders, schedules and shipping notices.

A 2026 post from Opendock, itself a vendor, says agentic dock and yard scheduling can reprioritize doors and trucks, but door assignments and exceptions still need human judgment. That supports a human review step before the plan is used.

Nail robots such as Nimble and Clockwork only apply liquid polish using cameras and a nozzle. None of them gives a full salon manicure with shaping or buffing, and none works with powdered polish and a buffer. They are robots in any case, which the reference AI agent is not.
Clockwork's robot paints nails with 3D cameras and AI in about 10 minutes. It is limited to polish cartridges, so it still needs physical hardware and cannot buff with powdered polish.
US state cosmetology boards generally require a license, with training hours and practical exams, to perform manicure services on clients.

In policing, AI tools such as Truleo and Polis turn body-worn-camera audio into text and flag unprofessional language or interactions. A preliminary randomized trial found that AI-led auditing changed officer conduct. This covers one sub-step: reviewing recorded footage.

Correctional sergeants supervise their officers in person. They make rounds of housing units, inspect units to confirm officers are doing their duties, and monitor staff morale. These rounds are logged and required at least once per shift.

Agency post orders require the area supervisor to make rounds and log them in person. The facility's chain of command holds the supervisor accountable for staff conduct and for any discipline that follows.
Inmate transport means putting restraints on prisoners, counting heads before departure and on arrival, and keeping them in sight for the whole escort. These are physical, in-person duties.
Agency policy requires two trained, weapons-qualified detention deputies on transports. Using only one deputy needs a supervisor's approval, so sworn humans are required by rule.
Software only helps with the surrounding steps, such as scheduling transports, checking the routing and doing paperwork. Making the actual transfer or driving the vehicle cannot be automated.

Stripping and refinishing a floor is hands-on work. A worker applies stripper, removes the old finish with a floor machine, a razor scraper and pads, picks up the slurry with a wet/dry vacuum, neutral-mops and puts down several coats of finish. A software-only agent can do none of these steps; at most it could look up procedures or chemical dilutions.

Even the floor machines themselves have limits here. Autoscrubbers cannot reach edges, corners or alcoves, so those areas need manual work. Stripping solution should also not be run through a scrubber's solution dispensing system.

A university custodial procedure has crews dust-mop and neutral-mop after stripping, then apply two finish layers with drying time between them. All of it is physical, on-site labour over several hours.

Cvent Event Diagramming (formerly Social Tables) has an AI assistant that builds room layouts from text prompts and can import event details from uploaded event orders (BEOs). This covers the planning step, but the room setup itself is still done by hand.

EventDiagram makes to-scale floor plans, seating charts and 3D views for hotels and venues, and shares them for approval. It produces a plan only: staff still have to move the furniture, set up the AV equipment and put up the decorations.

ChatDiagram generates scaled 2D event floor plans from a text description. This could speed up the layout sub-step for housekeeping staff, but most of the working time goes to physically arranging the room, which a software-only agent cannot do.

The task consists of hands-on work with hand tools and power equipment: string trimmers where mowers can't reach, aerating, dethatching, removing debris and spreading mulch. A software-only agent cannot do any of this physically.

The robotic mowers with edge-trimming arms shown in 2026 (Anthbot R7, Eufy S2 Max, Segway Navimow) are robots, which the reference technology excludes. Reviewers also say edge trimming is still largely unsolved for robot mowers.
O*NET describes this as routine field labor that also includes sod laying, mowing, digging and raking. None of these tasks needs a licence or a human sign-off; the barrier is purely physical.
Seismic's Aura Role-play Agent acts out live buyer scenarios, scores how reps perform, and gives coaching feedback on the spot. Its presentation agent puts together branded decks automatically.
Letter.ai says it builds interactive training modules in minutes and tailors coaching to the company's own products, customers and frameworks.

SalesHood's AI role-play builds simulations for sellers, sales engineers and customer success managers, including discovery and demo practice. Expert human judgment on how customers actually apply the technology still has to check the content and the coaching.

Vendor sources (self-reported marketing, not independently checked) say AI recruiting agents handle sourcing, screening, outreach and interview scheduling with little human input. They describe only preliminary AI-run assessments, not complete interviews or final hiring decisions done end to end.

The EU AI Act classes AI used in recruitment as high-risk. Employers must keep monitoring it and must have humans able to spot and correct errors, including discriminatory patterns, so a human has to stay in the loop on selection. According to a secondary source, these obligations may be postponed from 2 August 2026 to December 2027.
Commentary on the Act says that under Article 14 a policy document alone does not count as human oversight. Real people must be able to detect and correct errors.

Paint marks go on logs with handheld spray cans or with compressed-air sprayers mounted on processors. Either way, someone or something has to physically act on each log in the yard or on the line. A software-only agent can't do that.
When log marking is automated, it's done by sprayers built into harvesting or processing machinery. That's robotics and mill equipment, not an AI agent working through software.
Log scanners in mills, such as MiCROTEC Logeye, can grade logs. But they're fixed mill hardware, so they cover the grading decision, not the act of painting marks or calling out grades on site.

Oregon logging rules require hand signals or audible contact when noise, distance or poor visibility make voice unclear. Operators must not move loads unless the signal is clear, and all workers must be clear before a signal to move a log.

Idaho rules say that if the loading machine operator does not have an unobstructed view, a signalman must be properly placed in the loading area and their signal followed. Signals are standard hand signals, whistles or similar.
BC safe work procedures say all landing workers must be in view or in the clear, or their whereabouts known, before logs or equipment are moved. This is a real-time, line-of-sight, on-site judgement.

Construction firms already use AI assistants such as Skanska's Safety Sidekick, which combine company EHS manuals with OSHA construction standards to answer workers' safety questions. These tools help the worker; they do not do the learning or the compliance for the worker.

Research and commercial RAG chatbots, such as Turner's SafeT Coach and academic prototypes, find and explain OSHA clauses with high factual accuracy. They speed up the learning part of the task but leave a human in the loop.

OSHA 1926.1427 requires the operator personally to be certified through written and practical tests, and to be trained and evaluated as competent on the equipment. Safe operation on the jobsite is a physical duty the operator must carry out in person.

Electronic blasting systems such as Austin Powder's E*STAR check detonators before the blast and let firing data be downloaded and exported to a PC afterward. That digital record could help an AI confirm detonation, but it does not replace the blaster's own observation at the firing point.

MSHA rules require faces and muck piles to be checked for misfires after each blast. They also set waiting periods before anyone re-enters a blast area where a misfire is suspected. This makes confirming detonation a physical, on-site safety duty.
For surface coal mines, the rules say blasting must be under the direct control of authorized persons, and blasted areas must be examined for undetonated explosives after each blast.

Speed regulation in rolling mills is already handled by closed-loop automatic speed controllers and control computers that send speed presets. The operator watches the line and makes manual corrections for problems such as worn rolls or poor threading. This control is built into the plant's own automation, not done by a general AI agent.

Mill speed control is done through the plant's Level 1 PLC/HMI systems and operator desks. These are closed industrial control systems on the shop floor, and a software agent would not normally have access to them.
Automated rolling mill data is monitored continuously from operator desks and HMI systems in the control room, and operators are physically present at the line.

To take nicks out of a cutter with an oilstone, a person holds the edge on a coarse stone, presses firmly until the nicks are gone, then finishes on a finer stone. It is skilled work done by hand, so an agent with no physical body cannot do it. At most it could look up instructions.
Before honing, the worker looks at the edge to find nicks and check that it is straight. Oil on the stone carries away the metal filings. Every step means handling the tool and the stone directly.
Oilstones are sold as ordinary hand tools for shop use. No law or licence requires a person to do or sign off this work, so physical handling is the only thing stopping an agent.

Printing proofs from plates is still mostly done by hand. Operators pull sheets from the delivery and check them under standard lighting or with an optical instrument, and many printshops depend on experienced operators to judge makeready results.

Built-in inspection systems such as Fujifilm's Revoria PIS scan sheets and compare them with RIP data to find streaks, registration errors and density changes. This automates the quality-checking step, but only on equipped presses and through the press's own systems.

Press-integrated systems like RYOBI MHI's PQS-D catch plate-mounting mistakes and missing characters. These are machine functions, not something a software-only agent can do. Plate mounting, inking and running the proof press still need hands on the machine.

Orthotics and prosthetics CAD/CAM tools (Canfit, OMEGA, Rodin4D) use reusable digital templates, trimlines and rule-based shape changes. These can produce the dimensions and patterns ahead of time, but a person still has to put the marks on the physical part.
Wrapstyler creates pattern templates from 3D surfaces and replaces hand-drawn pattern making. This is digital help that comes before the hands-on layout work.
Scanning and design software builds 3D models that serve as templates for carving positive molds. The measuring and marking itself is still done by hand on real materials with precision instruments.

Under 14 CFR 43.3, maintenance is limited to authorised people. Pilots may do preventive maintenance only on aircraft they own or operate, and not on aircraft used under Part 121/135. The person who does the work signs the return to service (43.7), so a certificated human has to perform and sign it.

Electronic tech logs such as Thales Aviobook Techlog send pilots' defect entries straight to the airline's maintenance information system. This digitises the 'arrange for maintenance' part, but a pilot still makes and signs the entry.

Vendors advertise AI-assisted CMMS that move a pilot squawk through deferral triage to release to service. This speeds up arranging the work, but the hands-on minor maintenance still has to be done physically.

Load-optimization software such as ORTEC uses AI-driven logic for dimensions, weight, stacking rules and load stability. It produces 3D plans that serve as loading instructions and can connect to TMS, WMS and SAP systems.

ContainerMath uses AI to read packing lists and produce phone-friendly 2D dock views with weight distribution. This automates the planning part of the directions, but people on the dock still carry out the loading and supervise it.
Load planning systems produce labeled loading maps and loading sequences for drivers and dock workers to follow. The real-time verbal direction and checking at the trailer stay with a person on site.

Yard software such as GE RailConnect TMS and PST SwitchPro already automates car-movement tracking, switching sequences and work orders. An agent could parse switch lists and car schedules into a move plan, but the certified engineer still has to take in the plan and act on it in the cab.
Vendor yard-automation platforms cover hump, flat, receiving and departure yards, which shows that the planning and scheduling side can already be done in software.

Under FRA rules (49 CFR 240), anyone who moves a locomotive, including a remote-control operator, must be a certified engineer. The certified person who carries out the conductor's radio or in-person orders is accountable for understanding them.

Under federal rules (49 CFR 218.37), when a train stops on main track, a crew member with flagman's signals must walk back a set distance, place torpedoes on the rail and show a lighted fusee. The crew does this on site and is responsible for it under the regulation.

In practice, after an unplanned stop the conductor takes the flagging kit and walks back to protect the train unless the dispatcher (RTC) relieves the crew of flagging. Meanwhile the engineer radios the dispatcher. Directing and coordinating this happens on the spot, by voice and radio, during the emergency.

Flag protection is a GCOR operating rule (around Rules 6.19/6.20) that certified train crews carry out. Software could at most help by looking up the rules or drafting radio messages. No product was found that gives these instructions by itself.

Robotic refuelling systems such as Autofuel and a Russian pilot at Oillab rely on physical robot arms. They need vehicles to be pre-registered and fitted with special fuel caps the arm can grip. That is robotics, not a software agent, so an AI agent without a body cannot insert the nozzle or fill the tank.
A robot arm finds the fuel cap, inserts the nozzle and removes it when fuelling is done. This shows the core of the task is physical handling.

New Jersey's 1949 Retail Gasoline Dispensing Safety Act says only a trained attendant may dispense fuel. Sources from 2022–2023 say it was then the only US state with this rule. Most jurisdictions allow self-service, so there is no general licensing barrier. I did not confirm whether New Jersey's law has changed since 2023.
Pizza Ranch leased bussing robots to carry dirty dishes so human bussers could spend more time cleaning tables. Wiping tables stays a manual human job, and these are robots, not software agents.
Smile Robotics' ACUR-C bussing robot with an arm clears tables much more slowly than a human. Physical table work needs robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.
Automatic table wipers were still only a student prototype meant to replace the rag. I found no results from its planned trial.

Autonomous floor scrubbers are sold for restaurants and kitchens, for example the Cenobots L50/SP50 sold through Martin Bros. These are robots, and the reference agents have no robotics. The agents also can't polish counters, shelves, walls or equipment.

The Keenon KleenBot C40, marketed for restaurants and priced at $19,600, is physical robotic hardware. A software-only agent could at most schedule or monitor a robot like this, which is not the cleaning work itself.
A vendor recommends running robotic scrubbers in kitchens after hours. That confirms floor cleaning is physical work done on site.
O*NET lists this as a Dishwasher task. It means washing, peeling and cutting produce and other foods by hand in a kitchen.
In employer job postings, dishwasher food prep is hands-on work done in the kitchen, such as cleaning and peeling vegetables.

The O*NET duty list puts food prep (washing and cutting produce) next to physical kitchen work like running dish machines and storing items. A software-only agent can at most look up a recipe or prep list.

Ready-made landscaping safety documents already exist, such as Safe Work Method Statements, safe operating procedures for mowers and excavators, and OSHA-oriented checklists. An AI agent could draft and adapt this kind of written material from start to finish.

A landscaping supervisor is generally expected to enforce OSHA guidelines and company safety rules, including PPE use and safe chemical handling. They also train crews and record infractions. Much of this is done in person at job sites, which an agent without a body cannot do.

OSHA puts the duty to provide a safe workplace on the employer. One training vendor notes that only an employer can designate an employee as certified. However, no licence requires a human to personally write or sign the work standards themselves.

Landscape training platforms such as Greenius deliver course content on safe work and equipment operation, supply 110 weekly tailgate talks and track who has completed courses. They cover the digital materials and record-keeping side of training. A related OSHA-aligned course says the practical proficiency check is done hands-on by the employer.

An OSHA-aligned online landscaping course covers equipment use, chemical handling and PPE in theory. Practical evaluation is a separate in-person step, and only the employer can designate an employee as certified.

In states such as North Carolina, the licensed supervisor must make sure a non-certified pesticide applicator has recent training and has been taught to operate the equipment in the past year. Training is required by law for some sub-tasks, but the law does not say an AI cannot take part in it.

SingleOps' property measurement tool uses aerial photos to measure square footage. It feeds production rates and custom inputs such as labor rates, chemical usage and equipment usage into estimates. That covers the main sub-steps of working out labor and machine needs.

LMN, which merged with SingleOps, partnered with Attentive.ai on AI mapping and measurement to cut takeoff time. I found no product that turns a contract directly into crew and equipment assignments, so a supervisor still adds site and crew knowledge and checks the plan.

Aspire's commercial landscaping software includes estimating templates, scheduling and routing, and takeoff integrations. The task is document review and planning work done in systems an agent can reach, with no licence or sign-off required.

Fleet maintenance AI such as Fleetio's AI Service Advisor sorts repairs by priority, drafts service requests, approves low-risk work within set policies and handles routine follow-up. That covers the paperwork side of repairs, not the hands-on fixing or coaching of workers.

Landscaping fleet software can pull diagnostic data from telematics and track parts like oil filters and blade belts. Small equipment without telematics, such as walk-behind mowers and trimmers, is a gap, and the actual repair work stays physical.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.147 requires a written lockout/tagout program, a procedure for each machine and worker training. A supervisor has to coordinate this on site, but no licence or sign-off is required for small-engine repair.

Vendors sell AI receptionists for landscapers that answer service questions and give ballpark price ranges. Final pricing waits for an on-site estimate, and commercial or HOA inquiries go to a human sales rep.
AI answering services for landscaping companies handle calls, answer service questions and capture leads around the clock.

Landscape contractor licensing rules vary by state and apply to the business doing or bidding the work. None of the sources found require a licensed human to answer customer questions about methods, materials or price ranges.
USPS self-service kiosks handle some counter sales, such as stamps and postage labels, paid by card. Kiosks are dedicated hardware, not a software agent acting for the clerk.
Postal money orders are bought at Post Office locations with cash, a debit card or a traveler's check, not a credit card. That means handling cash and physical instruments at the counter.
Retail associates also help customers use the kiosks in person during business hours, so counter sales are still largely physical, face-to-face transactions.

MES systems already log production data, material usage, operator activity and process history automatically, and that record serves as the audit trail. Most of the transcription and compilation work in this task can therefore be done in software.
Infor MES documentation says automatic data collection cuts errors and improves timing accuracy compared with manual entry.

Vendors sell AI agents for manufacturing data entry, inspection logging and quality-record upkeep. These are marketing claims, not independent proof. Counts, gauge readings and checks on the shop floor still need someone there in person when sensors or PLC feeds are missing.

Google Document AI's human-in-the-loop feature uses confidence thresholds to send only uncertain extractions to human reviewers, who check and correct values before the data reaches business systems. Software already does most of the comparison, and people handle the exceptions.

RapidAutomation's verify_me block shows AI-extracted data next to the original source file. A reviewer accepts, rejects or edits the values, and the validated result is logged with a timestamp. This automates the side-by-side check with a human approving the output.

ABBYY markets human-in-the-loop verification for AI document processing to get higher precision. Vendors still keep a person reviewing low-confidence or exception fields, so full unattended verification is not yet standard.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person who is on site. The work itself must be done by trained, experienced employees that this person selects.

OSHA interpretations say the competent person must be on site to spot hazards and correct them, and that erectors face the physical hazards of working on a partly built structure. This makes the task hands-on physical work.

Scaffold software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer, scaffmax and Layher LayPLAN automates layout design and material lists. It only covers planning, which is a small side part of a laborer's erecting and dismantling work, not the physical assembly.

Pipe laying is done in the trench with physical equipment: a pipe laser projects a beam along the trench to set the gradient, and each pipe section is placed and aligned by hand against targets. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
To line up the laser and pipe, someone in the trench has to place and move physical targets on the pipe and read the beam against them.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, a competent person named by the employer must inspect the trench on site every day and after events like rainstorms, and must have authority to fix hazards. This keeps the work tied to a human on site.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.850, a competent person must do an engineering survey on site before workers start demolition. They must also check adjacent structures, shore or brace weakened walls and shut off utilities. All of this means being physically present.

AI tools for deconstruction planning mostly do research- or pilot-stage material assessment from scans, thermal imaging or drone data. The actual removal is still done by manual crews or future robots, not software agents.
Mattersite turns 3D scans and point clouds into pre-demolition material reports. Digital help is limited to inventory and estimates, not the work of tearing down buildings or salvaging materials.
Employer postings for septic and vacuum truck drivers require a commercial driver's license (Class A or B), often with a tanker endorsement. That means a licensed human must drive the vehicle.

Sewage truck operator postings ask for a Class B CDL at minimum, with endorsements depending on the truck's weight and waste capacity. The job is physically operating heavy vehicles, which a software-only AI agent can't do; it could only help with side work like route planning.
In septic pumper technician roles the same person drives the truck, carries equipment and crew, and does the on-site work, so the driving can't be split off to software.

Matching cable and cutter size to pipe diameter is a simple lookup in published charts (for example, 3/8-inch cable for 2-3 inch lines, 5/8-inch for 3-6 inch mains). The real work is fitting the cutter onto the cable by hand, which an AI agent cannot do.
Commercial drain machines come with physical cutter sets that a person mounts on the cable at the drum or reel. No software or AI product does this step.

Nokia's Gemini-powered Assurance Center agents (router agent and event triage agent) are already running and do network fault triage and diagnosis. Operators keep the final say over critical actions, and only low-risk cases are closed-loop automated.
TM Forum's Agentic NOC catalyst says current AIOps stops at recommendation and leaves humans to drive each step. Its goal of autonomous closed-loop remediation is still at project stage.

Remote testing is done in software: switches are reached over telnet or a remote maintenance system to run card and line diagnostics. Remote testing can isolate faults and avoid sending a technician, although some faults still need someone on site.
